raw_case_text: A 54-year-old gentleman with a history of well-controlled HIV established on Truvada and raltegravir, seizures, migraines, and previously treated syphilis presented to Croydon University Hospital with a 4-week history of progressive left leg weakness, bowel and bladder change, and a 1-week history of dysesthesia (Table 2). He denied any infective symptoms, weight loss, and personal or family history of tuberculosis (TB). He had no recent travel and reported no new sexual partners. Clinical examination revealed a normal cardiorespiratory examination. Neurologically, the patient had brisk reflexes in all limbs with reduced power (MRC 0/5) in the left leg combined with sensory dissociation starting from T5 in keeping with Brown-Sequard syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine undertaken at this time identified two peripherally enhancing cavitating lesions at T4-T5 with associated meningeal thickening and cord oedema. These images were felt indicative of CNS TB. Following this, anti-TB medication was started, and the patient was transferred to St. George's Hospital for further care. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis undertaken revealed highly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and white cell count (7 x 109/L). CSF cryptococcal antigen (CRAG), TB molecular testing (GeneXpert), microscopy and culture, and viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were all negative. Serial sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB), peripheral blood cultures, and Q-interferon tests were negative. At this point, syphilis serological testing was undertaken; this suggested highly active acute infection (serum EIA positive and rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (1 in 64)). CSF serology showed positive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) 10240 and RPR 1 in 2 suggesting active disease. This raised the possibility of neurosyphilis with spinal syphilitic gumma. Due to no conclusive TB diagnosis, concurrent neurosyphilis treatment was initiated by way of 14-day high-dose benzylpenicillin therapy commencing on day 11 of presentation. Repeat MRI of the spine on days 12 and 22 of admission revealed incremental improvement in both spinal cord oedema and the size of the T4-T5 lesions (Figure 1). Following this, positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was performed on day 41 which showed no significant areas of increased uptake outside of the spine for potential biopsy. This improvement in the spinal disease was associated with progressive and marked improvements in his neurology, and by day 55, the patient could walk several lengths of parallel bars from being previously bedbound.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old HIV-positive man presented with a 4-week history of progressive left lower-extremity weakness and bowel and bladder dysfunction, accompanied by a 1-week history of dysesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 weeks, the patient developed progressive left leg paralysis and neurogenic bowel/bladder changes, followed 1 week prior to presentation by truncal/limb dysesthesia below T5. Initial spinal MRI suggested CNS tuberculosis and empiric anti-TB therapy was started prior to transfer, until syphilis serology and CSF testing confirmed spinal syphilitic gumma.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of well-controlled HIV infection on Truvada (tenofovir/emtricitabine) and raltegravir, epilepsy/seizures, migraines, and previously treated syphilis. Denied personal/family history of tuberculosis, recent travel, or new sexual partners.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive left leg weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and T5 sensory dysesthesia; negative for fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Home medications: Truvada and raltegravir.

objective.physical_examination: Cardiorespiratory examination was normal. Neurological examination demonstrated a classic T5 Brown-Sequard hemicord syndrome: severe left lower-limb paralysis (MRC power 0/5), generalized brisk deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, and dissociated sensory loss below the T5 dermatome.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial sputum acid-fast bacilli smears, peripheral blood cultures, and QuantiFERON-TB testing were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine MRI demonstrated two peripherally enhancing cavitating intramedullary lesions at T4-T5 with adjacent meningeal thickening and spinal cord edema. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed markedly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and pleocytosis (WBC 7 x 10^9/L [7 cells/uL]), with negative CSF cryptococcal antigen, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, AFB smear/culture, and viral PCRs. Day 41 whole-body FDG PET/CT showed no extraspinal hypermetabolic lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed T4-T5 intramedullary spinal syphilitic gummas presenting with Brown-Sequard syndrome in an HIV-positive patient (spinal tuberculoma excluded via negative GeneXpert, AFB cultures, and QuantiFERON), established via positive serum treponemal EIA, serum RPR titer of 1:64, positive CSF TPPA (titer 1:10,240), and reactive CSF RPR (titer 1:2). Commenced on hospital day 11 on a 14-day course of high-dose intravenous benzylpenicillin. Repeat spinal MRIs on days 12 and 22 showed progressive regression of the T4-T5 cavitary gummas and cord edema, and by hospital day 55 he had progressed from complete paraplegia/bedbound status to walking in parallel bars.
